stages.title: The rule reads fine
stages.desc: Customers, the restaurant, and riders can read an order.
stages.narration: Riders need to see orders. The rule says customers, owners, and riders.

stages.title: The review is clean
stages.desc: One reviewer, one identity. The app only asks for the right orders.
stages.narration: The review comes back clean. The app never asks for the wrong order.

stages.title: The exploit path
stages.desc: Sign in as any rider. Read orders/{any id}. Get a stranger’s phone and address.
stages.narration: Now the path: any rider reads any order, with the phone and address.

stages.title: A role is not ownership
stages.desc: isRider() checks the caller. It never compares the order to the caller.
stages.narration: A role is not ownership. The order is never checked.

stages.title: Pen test: two riders
stages.desc: riderA is assigned o-1. riderB reads it. The test expects denied.
stages.narration: The pen test signs in as a second rider. The read succeeds.

stages.title: The fix, and the test stays
stages.desc: isAssignedRider() compares rider.id to request.auth.uid. The test runs on every push.
stages.narration: The rule now checks the assigned rider. The test stays in CI.

stages.title: Cyber: blast radius
stages.desc: Rank credentials by what an attacker can do, not by how visible they are.
stages.status: FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT first · API key public by design
stages.narration: The cybersecurity agent ranks credentials by blast radius, not by visibility.

stages.title: Three agents disagree
stages.desc: The review passed it. The attack failed it. That disagreement is the point.
stages.narration: Three agents, on purpose. The review passed it. The attack did not.

stages.title: Read the rules, then attack them
stages.desc: An exploit path per finding, credentials by blast radius, two accounts per role.
stages.narration: Read the rules. Then attack them.

end.title: Read the rules. Then attack them.
end.sub: A permissive rule and a correctly behaving app look identical from inside the app.

post.caption:
The Firestore rule read fine. Any rider could read any order. 🗡️

A food delivery app with three roles. Riders need to see orders, so the rule says: customer, restaurant owner, or rider. A review reads it and comes back clean.

But isRider() checks the caller's role and never compares the order to the caller. Every order carries the customer's name, phone and address. Sign in as any rider, read any order, and you have a stranger's home address.

Three security agents, on purpose:
🛡️ Security: no finding without an exploit path. Who signs in, what they ask, what comes back.
🔑 Cybersecurity: credentials ranked by blast radius. The CI service account first; the Firebase API key is public by design.
🗡️ Pen test: two accounts per role, and attack tests that run on every push.

Full article: blog.msdevbuild.com/blog/ai-agents-security-cybersecurity-penetration-testing
